seoTitle: How to Set Up a Loan in QuickBooks Easily (2026)
metaDescription: Set up a loan in QuickBooks Online: the right account type and detail type, what to put in the opening balance field, and how to split payments correctly.
intro: Recording a loan incorrectly in QuickBooks can throw off your liability tracking and interest expense reporting down the line, and the setup isn't a dedicated "loan wizard". It's a liability account you configure by hand. This guide covers opening the Chart of accounts, creating that liability account with the right type and detail type, and entering the opening balance so QuickBooks tracks the loan correctly from day one. It's aimed at small business owners and accountants managing lending or borrowing activity who want the account set up right the first time.
prerequisites: A QuickBooks Online account with permission to create new accounts
The loan's principal amount, start date, and payment schedule from your lender

steps.heading: Open the Chart of accounts
steps.body: Sign in to QuickBooks Online and open Chart of accounts, found under the left-hand Accounting menu, or under All apps > Accounting if you're on the newer navigation. This is where every account QuickBooks tracks lives: bank accounts, accounts receivable, and liabilities, each showing its current balance. A loan isn't created anywhere else in the interface; it starts here as a new liability account, so this list is your starting point regardless of how the loan will eventually be paid down.

image.caption: The Chart of accounts, listing every bank, asset, and liability account in QuickBooks with its current balance. A new loan account is added from here.

steps.heading: Create the liability account with the matching detail type
steps.body: Click New account and give it a specific name, such as "Office Equipment Loan" instead of something generic like "Loan", which matters once you're tracking more than one over time. QuickBooks pairs each loan account type with one specific detail type: choose Long Term Liabilities with the Notes Payable detail type if repayment runs past a year, or Other Current Liabilities with the Loan Payable detail type if the loan is due within twelve months. Notes Payable is the detail type Intuit's own help article names for a long-term loan; "Other Long Term Liabilities" is not the detail type currently documented for this.

image.caption: The New account panel, naming the account "Office Equipment Loan" and setting its type to Long Term Liabilities with a matching detail type.

steps.heading: Enter the opening balance the right way
steps.body: The field for this is labeled Opening balance, not Unpaid balance. What you put in it depends on when you're doing this. If the lender just deposited funds and you're recording the loan from scratch, leave Opening balance at $0 and record the deposit in the next step instead, since filling it in here as well would count the loan twice. If you're adding a loan that's already partway through repayment, enter the current balance as of today, not the original loan amount. QuickBooks posts any beginning balance to Opening Balance Equity to keep the books in balance, so using the original amount here overstates what you still owe.

steps.heading: Record where the loan proceeds went
steps.body: A liability account by itself only tracks what you owe. It doesn't move any money on its own. If the lender deposited funds into your bank account, record a bank deposit or journal entry that increases your bank balance and offsets it against the new liability account, so both sides of the transaction show up. If the loan paid for something directly, such as equipment bought through the lender, record that purchase against the liability account instead of a bank account.

steps.heading: Set up payments split between principal and interest
steps.body: A loan payment usually isn't one lump expense: part reduces the liability balance and part is a genuine interest cost. Record each payment (a check, in QuickBooks' own example) split across two lines, one against the loan liability account for the principal and one against an interest expense account for the interest. If the loan runs on a fixed schedule, setting this up as a recurring transaction under Recurring transactions saves you from re-splitting the amounts by hand every cycle.

steps.heading: Monitor the loan through reports
steps.body: Once payments start posting, check the Balance Sheet periodically to watch the liability balance decline, and run a Profit and Loss report to see the interest expense build up over time. Comparing the liability balance against your lender's own amortization schedule every few months is worth doing: a mismatch usually means a payment was split incorrectly between principal and interest, not an actual discrepancy with the lender.

troubleshooting.problem: The loan's opening balance doesn't match what you owe
troubleshooting.cause: The original loan amount was entered for a loan that's already partway through repayment, or a deposit was recorded separately on top of a nonzero opening balance for a brand-new loan.
troubleshooting.fix: For an existing loan, edit the opening balance to the current amount owed as of today. For a new loan, set the opening balance to $0 and record the lender's deposit as its own transaction.

troubleshooting.problem: An unexpected entry shows up in Opening Balance Equity
troubleshooting.cause: QuickBooks automatically posts any nonzero opening balance you enter when creating an account to Opening Balance Equity, to keep the chart of accounts in balance.
troubleshooting.fix: This is expected behavior for existing loans. If the amount looks wrong, correct the account's opening balance instead of editing Opening Balance Equity directly.

troubleshooting.problem: The liability balance doesn't go down after a payment
troubleshooting.cause: The payment was recorded entirely against an expense account, or the principal and interest weren't split across two lines.
troubleshooting.fix: Edit the transaction so one line hits the loan liability account for the principal and a separate line hits an interest expense account for the interest.

faq.question: Does QuickBooks Online have a dedicated loan setup wizard?
faq.answer: No. A loan is set up as a Long Term Liabilities or Other Current Liabilities account created from the Chart of accounts, with the detail type, opening balance, and payment splits configured manually.

faq.question: Should I use Long Term or Other Current Liabilities for a loan?
faq.answer: Use Other Current Liabilities with the Loan Payable detail type if the loan is due within a year, and Long Term Liabilities with the Notes Payable detail type if repayment extends beyond that.

faq.question: What do I put in the opening balance field?
faq.answer: Zero, if you're recording a brand-new loan and will enter the lender's deposit as a separate transaction. The current amount still owed, not the original loan amount, if you're adding a loan that's already partway through repayment.

faq.question: How do I record a loan payment correctly?
faq.answer: Split each payment across two lines: the principal portion reduces the loan liability account, and the interest portion posts to an interest expense account. Recording the whole payment against one account misstates either your liability or your expenses.

faq.question: How do I check that a loan is being tracked correctly?
faq.answer: Check the Balance Sheet for the declining liability balance and run a Profit and Loss report for accumulated interest expense, comparing both against your lender's amortization schedule periodically.
